segments.text: Crime theories explain why offending occurs by focusing on different causes or mechanisms.

Biological and psychological approaches focus on individual factors; sociological theories emphasize environment, structure and interaction. Social disorganization links crime with weakened community controls; strain with blocked goals/pressures; social control with weakened bonds; learning with learned definitions/behaviours; labeling with social reaction and identity processes.

Modern biological criminology investigates whether genetic, neurological, developmental and physiological factors contribute to differences in behaviour. These factors are probabilistic and interact with environment; they do not create a deterministic “criminal type.” Historical biological theories that linked criminality to physical appearance are now important mainly as examples of flawed scientific reasoning and harmful stereotyping.

Psychological theories examine cognition, personality, self-control, learning, trauma, moral development and decision-making. Evidence may identify group-level associations, but psychological assessment cannot replace legal proof of an offence.

Social disorganization theory links neighbourhood crime patterns to weakened local social control under conditions such as concentrated disadvantage, population turnover and disrupted community networks. Strain theories examine pressure created when valued goals or needs cannot be achieved through legitimate means or when individuals experience adverse conditions. Social control theories ask why people conform and emphasize bonds, supervision and commitment.

Social learning theories focus on how definitions, techniques and rewards for offending are learned through interaction. Labeling theory studies how social reaction and stigmatizing identities can influence later behaviour and opportunities. Each theory explains part of the crime problem; none is a universal law.

blocks.text: Integrating theory and an Islamic perspective

segments.text: An Islamic perspective can discuss moral agency, accountability, justice, protection of life and property, social responsibility, prevention and reformation. It can also examine how family, community, economic fairness and ethical education relate to crime prevention. It should be presented as a normative and socio-legal perspective, not as a substitute for empirical testing of causal claims.

In an analytical answer, compare theories by unit of analysis, mechanism and policy implication. For example: social disorganization points toward neighbourhood capacity; learning theory toward peer networks and reinforcement; control theory toward bonds and supervision; strain theory toward pressures and legitimate opportunities.

items.text: Every theory should answer the same question:
what mechanism does it propose between conditions and offending? Memorizing the theorist's name without that mechanism produces weak answers.

Biological approaches examine inherited, neurological or physiological factors; psychological approaches examine cognition, personality, development or mental processes; sociological approaches focus on groups, institutions and social structure.

Social disorganization emphasizes weakened community institutions and informal control. Strain theories focus on pressures created by blocked goals or stressful conditions. Social-control theories ask why people conform and point to weakened bonds or restraints.

Learning theories explain crime as behaviour, definitions and techniques learned through interaction. Labeling theory shifts attention to social reaction and how official labels can shape identity and future behaviour.
For each theory add one criticism:
reductionism, measurement limits, inability to explain all offence types, neglect of agency or structure, or limited generalizability. Then show where the theory may still be useful.

rows: Common confusion to avoid: Do not present any theory as a proven universal cause of crime. Criminological theories are explanatory models with strengths and limitations.

items.text: For every theory learn originator(s), main proposition, causal mechanism, criticism and application.
Do not present theories as proven universal laws.

segments.text: Different theories explain different dimensions of offending.
A strong answer compares theories rather than merely listing them.
Islamic perspective should be presented through verified normative/legal concepts, not invented quotations.
